wine.name: Forster Kirchenstück G.C.
wine.classification: G.C., the estate's own Grand Cru rank; the site is a VDP.Grosse Lage
wine.sites: The Kirchenstück, a small vineyard directly behind the church of Forst, enclosed by walls and the sandstone houses of the village, which hold the day's warmth: a gentle slope falling towards the village, on basalt, sandstone, limestone rubble and clay over a bank of limestone.
wine.making: From vines farmed biodynamically across the whole estate since 2005. Like every G.C. wine of the house, it ferments with wild yeasts and is raised only in large oak casks before it is bottled dry.
wine.glass: White peach, lime zest and pink grapefruit over wet stone and a faint smoky note; dry, taut and finely textured, with bright acidity, a salty grip and a long, tightly wound finish.
wine.ageing: Reserved for its first five years or so, it opens slowly and keeps for twenty years and more in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large white wine glass.

label.means: Grand Cru: the highest rank in the estate's own classification of its vineyards, not a term of German wine law.
The church piece: the walled vineyard beside the church of Forst.
The Mittelhaardt village between Wachenheim and Deidesheim where the Kirchenstück lies.

records.table: Beside the church at Forst lies the small walled Kirchenstück, which a Bavarian survey of 1828, by the estate's account, placed above every other site; Dr. Bürklin-Wolf bottles its dry Riesling as Forster Kirchenstück G.C. Fermented with wild yeasts in large casks, it is taut, smoky and long.
records.story: The house traces its roots in Wachenheim to 1597, and its history names a Bürklin of that age, a town clerk who became mayor of Wachenheim. The modern estate began with a marriage. In 1875 Albert Bürklin (1844 to 1924), a lawyer who later sat in the Reichstag, married a daughter of the Wolf family of Wachenheim, and her family's vineyards in Wachenheim, Forst, Deidesheim and Ruppertsberg came together under both names. He moved to Wachenheim and built the estate up. In 1924 it passed to a great nephew of the same name, Albert Bürklin (1907 to 1979), who by the estate's account led the rebuilding of Pfalz wine after the Second World War and added vineyards and cellars; his eldest daughter took over in 1990. Long before, in 1828, a royal Bavarian survey had ranked the vineyards of the Pfalz for land tax, and the estate records that the Kirchenstück alone received the highest mark. In the 1990s the house made that survey the base of its own ladder, in the manner of Burgundy, printing G.C. and P.C. on its labels, and by 2005 the whole estate was farmed biodynamically. The Kirchenstück stands at the summit of that ladder: a small walled vineyard read as a Grand Cru, though German law knows no such word.

The making rests on the estate's terroir page, which says every G.C. wine is fermented with wild yeasts and raised only in large oak casks; no sheet for the Kirchenstück alone gave a cask size or a time in wood, so none is given.
The year the estate began its own ranking is 1990 on its terroir page and 1994 in Wein.plus and Skurnik, so the story says the 1990s; 2005 for biodynamics rests on Skurnik and Vinello.

Luise Wolf's dates (1848 to 1882) were found in one source only, so she is described, not named; the Bürklin of 1597, a town clerk and mayor whom the estate dates 1580 to 1636, is described because the estate alone gives him.
That the 1828 survey gave the Kirchenstück alone its highest mark is the estate's claim, told as the estate records it; the library's wine note says the same.

wine.name: Forster Jesuitengarten Riesling Grosses Gewächs
wine.classification: VDP.Grosses Gewächs: the dry wine of a VDP.Grosse Lage, the association's highest site rank
wine.sites: The Jesuitengarten at Forst, named for the old Jesuit house of Neustadt that owned it, on sandy loam, sandstone rubble, marly clay and basalt.
wine.making: The grapes are pressed gently and the must is split: part ferments with the vineyard's own yeasts in traditional oak Stückfass casks, part in stainless steel. Both stay on their lees until bottling, and the wine is bottled dry.
wine.glass: Ripe yellow peach, orange zest and pear over honeysuckle and a smoky, stony thread; dry yet broad and juicy, more perfume than grip, with ripe acidity, ending long and savoury.
wine.ageing: Open and generous within a few years of the vintage, it keeps and deepens for fifteen years and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; half an hour in a decanter opens a young bottle; a large glass for white wine.

records.table: The Jesuits who once owned the vineyard gave their name to Bassermann-Jordan's Forster Jesuitengarten Riesling, a dry Grosses Gewächs, broad, ripe and gently smoky, for roast pork or river fish. Part of it ferments in traditional oak casks with its own yeasts.
records.story: Andreas Jordan (1775 to 1848) made the estate that a Jordan forebear had founded in 1718, as its own history has it: he took it over at twenty after his parents' deaths and built a house of quality from shrinking assets. He is credited with selling, from 1802, Pfalz wine named for its village and its vineyard. He died in 1848 without a will, and his estate was divided equally among his three children; from the shares came three houses, Jordan, Buhl and Deinhard, the last of them the estate that became von Winning. From 1899 two brothers ran the house together under the Bassermann-Jordan name, Ludwig Bassermann-Jordan (1869 to 1914) and Friedrich von Bassermann-Jordan (1872 to 1959). Friedrich published his history of viticulture, the work that made his name, in 1907, and in 1910 the brothers were among the founders of the association of natural wine auctioneers from which the VDP grew. The vaulted cellar beneath the estate keeps old vintages back to 1811. In 2002 the estate was sold to a Neustadt entrepreneur. The Jesuitengarten gathers the Jordan inheritance: a Forst site, a house of 1718, and the habit of naming a wine for its vineyard.

report: Read through search summaries of the estate's own pages (Pioniergeist, Herkunft and the shop sheets of the 2024 and 2025 Jesuitengarten), the VDP's site page and secondary accounts (Wein.plus, Meininger, KuLaDig, the Rheinland-Pfälzische Bibliographie, the history society GGW, Decanter, Wines of Germany); 6 of the author's 35 searches went to this house.

The estate names its founder of 1718 Pierre Jordan, while the KuLaDig monument record names a Johann Peter Jordan with dates (1753 to 1795) that cannot fit 1718, so the founder is described as a Jordan forebear.

Andreas Jordan's dates rest on the estate's own page and KuLaDig; the sale of wine by village and vineyard from 1802 is in two accounts (Wines of Germany and Wein.plus) and is told as a credit, not a proven first.
The elder brother, Ludwig (1869 to 1914), has dates in one source only and is described; Friedrich's dates are in Wein.plus and the regional bibliography, his book of 1907 in Wein.plus and the GGW.
The cellar's vintages back to 1811 rest on Meininger, KuLaDig and an importer; Decanter's report of an 1811 Forster Ungeheuer opened for the three hundredth year is one source and is left out.

Left out for want of a second source: the family's purchase of the Jesuitengarten in 1793 (the estate's Herkunft page alone), the move to Deidesheim in 1783 (KuLaDig alone), and the buyer's name, a man who died in 2013, given in one record only with dates.
The house is not in the library; the estate's sheets give the cask and steel split as part and part, varying by vintage, so no share is given.

wine.name: Forster Pechstein Riesling Grosses Gewächs
wine.classification: VDP.Grosses Gewächs from the Pechstein, a VDP.Grosse Lage of Forst
wine.sites: The Pechstein at Forst, named for its black basalt: rubble from the Pechsteinkopf, an old volcano above the slope, mixed with weathered red sandstone and clay, and basalt brought from an old quarry nearby.
wine.making: Fermented mostly in the Doppelstück, the 2400 litre oak cask of the Rhine lands, with a small part in stainless steel; the wine is then bottled dry, as every Grosses Gewächs must be.
wine.glass: Smoke, struck flint and crushed stone over lime, white peach and lemon peel; dry and taut, darker and more savoury than its Forst neighbours, with firm acidity and a salty finish.
wine.ageing: Closed and smoky in youth, it opens after five years or so and keeps for fifteen to twenty.
wine.serve: 11 to 12 degrees Celsius; an hour in a decanter helps a young bottle; a tall white wine glass.

records.table: The black basalt of an old volcano above Forst gives its smoke to Reichsrat von Buhl's Forster Pechstein Riesling, which ferments mostly in large oak casks. Dry and darker voiced than its Forst neighbours, it is a match for grilled fish.
records.story: The Deidesheim estate of Andreas Jordan, split among his three children after his death in 1848, gave this house its start: in 1849 Franz Peter Buhl (1809 to 1862), who had married Jordan's daughter, founded it with her share. His son, Franz Armand Buhl (1837 to 1896), inherited it, and the estate holds that its wine was poured for the toast at the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869. He took the name to the Reichstag, where he sat from 1871 to 1893 and helped to shape the first German wine law of 1892, above all its ban on adulterated wine. The title of Reichsrat, borne by the family, stayed in the estate's name. In 1989 the estate was leased to a Japanese businessman, a lease that ran until 2013; during it, in 2005, an entrepreneur from Neustadt bought the estate, and when the lease ended a new team took over the cellar. The Pechstein, its basalt shed by the Pechsteinkopf and brought from a quarry, gives a darker, smokier wine than its neighbours. What basalt adds to Forst is plain in it, above all beside a Kirchenstück or a Jesuitengarten.

The Pechstein's basalt is partly native, shed by the Pechsteinkopf, and partly brought from an old quarry nearby.

report: Read through search summaries of the estate's own page, the VDP's site page, the Deutsche Biographie, a mirror copy of the Wikipedia article (cited at its Wikipedia address), KuLaDig and two importers' sheets (SommSelect and a Mundi sheet); 6 of the author's 35 searches went to this house, one of them wasted.

The making rests on SommSelect (spontaneous fermentation in the Doppelstück, fine lees) and the Mundi sheet (the main part in Doppelstück, a small part in steel); no estate sheet was found, and the bottling in the summer after the harvest, in one source, is left out.

The sources disagree on who received the title Reichsrat and when (Franz Armand under the Bavarian crown, or his son with the name added in 1912), so the record says only that the family bore it; the son, Franz Eberhard (1867 to 1921), has dates in one source and is not named.

Left out for want of a source: the wines at the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 and Bismarck's friendship (one source), the organic certification (2009 and 2015 both given), and the Champagne cellar master of 2013 to 2019 (named only in a writer's own site and a blog).

Living or unsettled names met and kept out: the Japanese lessee, named in one source, the cellar master from Champagne, and the present winemaker; the buyer of 2005 died in 2013 and is described, his dates being in one record only.
The plan's 'Forster Pechstein Riesling' is kept as the name; labels and shops print it as Pechstein GG with Forst or Forster, and the record's label lists only Reichsrat, Pechstein and GG.

wine.name: Rieslaner Auslese Herzog
wine.classification: Prädikatswein, Auslese: selected ripe bunches, from the Herzog, a VDP.Erste Lage
wine.grapes: Rieslaner alone, a crossing of Silvaner and Riesling bred in Franconia in 1921.
wine.sites: The Herzog at Haardt, on the edge of Neustadt, a VDP.Erste Lage on Haardt sandstone, where the estate grows the Rieslaner it bottles as Auslese, Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese.
wine.making: Picked by hand, with a share of noble rot in many years, then fermented cool in stainless steel so that the fruit and the grape's high acidity stay bright; the wine is bottled sweet, at a moderate alcohol.
wine.glass: Ripe peach, mango and lime over honey, eucalyptus and dried hay, with a mushroomy touch of noble rot; sweet and full, cut through by vivid acidity, finishing clean, tangy and long.
wine.ageing: Lovely young for its fruit, it gains depth for many years, its high acidity holding the sweetness in line.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a small white wine glass and a small pour.

label.means: The grape: a crossing of Silvaner and Riesling, not a kind of Riesling.
Selected harvest: the Prädikat for very ripe bunches, here made as a sweet wine.
The vineyard at Haardt, an Erste Lage in the VDP's ranking of sites.

records.table: Not Riesling but Rieslaner, a crossing of Silvaner and Riesling, goes into Müller-Catoir's Rieslaner Auslese Herzog, a sweet wine grown on sandstone at Haardt. Mango, peach and honey ride on piercing acidity, so it can close a meal with a fruit tart.
records.story: According to the estate, the Catoirs, a Huguenot family, have grown wine at Haardt, on the edge of Neustadt, since 1744. In 1968, the estate relates, an heir took over a property split by inheritance and, over some forty years, brought it back into one hand. With a cellar master who served the house from the early 1960s until the early 2000s, he raised its standing: they gave as much care to Scheurebe, Muskateller and Rieslaner as to Riesling, and the wines they made were vivid and aromatic. Rieslaner was bred in Franconia in 1921 from Silvaner and Riesling and approved for planting in the Pfalz in 1968; it keeps high acidity, catches noble rot readily, and is grown mainly in Franconia and the Pfalz. Older bottlings of the estate named other sites, the Bürgergarten among them, but its own list leads its Rieslaner from the Herzog, a site on Haardt sandstone, as Auslese, Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese, a ladder of sweetness from one vineyard. Pour it for the guest who asks to move past Riesling: a German sweet wine from a crossing rather than from Riesling itself.

report: SWAP PROPOSED, of the wine and not the house: the plan's 'Haardter Bürgergarten Rieslaner' is not the bottling the estate leads with. Its own pages sell its Rieslaner as 'Rieslaner Auslese Herzog' (and Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese Herzog) from the Haardter Herzog, a VDP.Erste Lage on Haardt sandstone, and an importer (Bibendum) says the long serving cellar master planted Rieslaner in the Herzog; the Bürgergarten, a VDP.Erste Lage by the estate's vineyard page, gives its dry Riesling, and a Bürgergarten Rieslaner appears only as an old Beerenauslese on Vivino.

This record is therefore written for 'Rieslaner Auslese Herzog', and the lint's two problems on this record (wine.name and the table not holding the plan's words) stand until the chunk's checker agrees and changes the pick's wine in plan.json to 'Rieslaner Auslese Herzog'; the key and producerId need not change.

Read through search summaries of the estate's own About, vineyard, product and press pages, Wikipedia and Wein.plus on the grape, the Bibendum and Skurnik listings; 6 of the author's 35 searches went to this house.

The library's p-muller-catoir lists 'Haardter Bürgergarten Riesling GG' as the leading dry wine, but the estate's own vineyard page lists the Bürgergarten as a VDP.Erste Lage, from which a Grosses Gewächs cannot come; the library's wine list gives 'Rieslaner Auslese' with no site, which this record names.

The heir who took over in 1968 died in 2023 and his birth year was not found, so he is described; the cellar master of 1962 to 2002 (dates from one importer) is described, his living status not settled; the founder named on the estate's page, Johann Wilhelm Catoir, has no dates and is not named; the present owner is living and not named.

Left out for want of a second source: that the cellar master brought Rieslaner to the estate, Rieslaner's release for the Pfalz in 1968 (the estate's press page alone), an exact Auslese must weight and a time on the lees.

changed: story: the estate's belief that the Catoirs had worked vines in France is cut, since one account has the family tanners who first held Haardt as a country seat; the neoclassical enlargement of the manor around 1900 is cut, found in no source of this check.
story: the long serving cellar master is now dated from the early 1960s until the early 2000s, as accounts give 1961 or 1962 to 2001 or 2002 (Grapeguru, the Wein.plus wine guide).
story: Rieslaner's approval for planting in the Pfalz in 1968 is added, by Wikipedia and Wein.plus with the estate's press page.

story, wine.sites, traps[2] and cards[1]: the record no longer says the estate's Rieslaner never came from the Bürgergarten, since one account names Bürgergarten and Mussbacher Eselshaut Rieslaners and the author met a Bürgergarten Beerenauslese; it now says the estate's own list leads its Rieslaner from the Herzog.

The Herzog is a VDP.Erste Lage on the estate's own page; one outside account calls it a Grosse Lage. The estate's word stands.
The heir of 1968 and his forty years of reuniting the estate rest on the estate's page alone, told as its account.

The author's report says no Grosses Gewächs can come from the Bürgergarten; the estate's page shows one from its Breumel parcel, so the library's Haardter Bürgergarten Riesling GG is near enough right and needs no report.

records.place: Schweigen, Pfalz, from vines across the border at Wissembourg in Alsace

wine.name: Spätburgunder Kammerberg Grosses Gewächs
wine.classification: VDP.Grosses Gewächs from the Kammerberg, a VDP.Grosse Lage
wine.grapes: Spätburgunder, the German name for Pinot Noir, alone.
wine.sites: The Kammerberg, part of the Schweigener Sonnenberg on the French side of the border: a slope falling south towards Wissembourg at up to 30 per cent, on weathered limestone, loam and clay over pure limestone.
wine.making: The berries are destemmed and fermented in open wooden vats, the cap punched down each day; the mash is then carried to the press by hand and pressed gently. The wine matures slowly in French oak barriques, for up to twenty months, before bottling.
wine.glass: Sour cherry, wild strawberry and red currant over clove, smoke and a cool, chalky stoniness; fine grained and taut, with fresh acidity, toast from the barrique in youth and a long, savoury close.
wine.ageing: Tight and marked by its oak for its first five years, it opens with time in bottle and lasts fifteen years and more.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; an hour's decanting suits a young bottle; a wide Burgundy glass.

label.means: The German name for Pinot Noir; later labels may print Pinot Noir instead.
The initials under which the estate's later labels name the Kammerberg, its parcel in France.
Often shortened to GG: a dry wine of the VDP from a vineyard it ranks Grosse Lage.
The German region on the label, though the Kammerberg's vines stand across the border in France.

records.table: Just across the border in Alsace, on limestone, grow the vines of Friedrich Becker's Spätburgunder Kammerberg, yet the wine is sold as Pfalz from Schweigen. Destemmed, fermented in open wooden vats and raised in French barriques, it is cherry fruited, chalky and fine grained.
records.story: Until the 1970s the Beckers of Schweigen ran a mixed farm on the southern edge of the Pfalz and sold their wine to the village cooperative. In 1973 the son who took over from his parents left the cooperative and filled the first bottles under the family's own name, with a fox from one of Aesop's fables on the label, in the estate's own story. He turned to Spätburgunder, which the estate says has grown on these limestone slopes for centuries. Those slopes are the heart of the story. The Schweigener Sonnenberg runs over the border into France, and the Kammerberg lies on its French side, facing Wissembourg, yet its wine is made at Schweigen and sold as Pfalz. Benedictine monks of the abbey at Wissembourg once kept Kammerweine from it in their cellar; the site then lay forgotten until 1965, when, by the VDP's account and the estate's, a Becker took it up again. So the Kammerberg makes a favourite trap: a German Grosses Gewächs grown in France.

traps: The Kammerberg lies in France, at Wissembourg, yet the wine is labelled Pfalz: it is a parcel of the Schweigener Sonnenberg on the French side, farmed and pressed from Schweigen.
Spätburgunder is Pinot Noir under its German name, not a late harvest wine.
Kammerberg and Sankt Paul are parcels within the Schweigener Sonnenberg, not villages of their own.

sources.title: The Irish Times: Run for the border wine

report: Read through search summaries of the estate's own family, welcome and red wine pages, the VDP's pages on the Kammerberg and on the estate, and secondary accounts (The Irish Times and Meininger on the border rule, Rudi Wiest Selections and Discover Germany on the cooperative, Wein.plus on the Sonnenberg's parcels, Falstaff and Symbolic Wines on the KB label, Le Baroudeur du Vin on the barrels); 7 of the author's 35 searches went to this house.

founded is 1973, the year the family began to bottle its own wine, on the estate's page and two importers' accounts; the family farmed here for generations before, so the founding is that of the wine estate, and a checker may prefer it empty.

The founder is not named: one source (weinkenner.de) reports his death on 25 February 2025 at 77 and a second search did not confirm it, so his status is not settled; his son, who has run the estate since 2005, is living. The house keeps its name, Friedrich Becker, as a house.

The barrique's length is not given: Falstaff lists 24 months for the KB of 2020 alone, and the share of whole bunches (one retailer) is left out; the estate's own page gives destemming, open vats, hand pressing and young oak.

The legal basis of the border rule was not found in a primary text; The Irish Times and Meininger both report that the French side may be sold as German and not the reverse, so the record states the rule without naming a law.

The plan's wording 'Spätburgunder Kammerberg' is kept as the name, though older labels print 'Schweigener Kammerberg Spätburgunder' and later ones 'KB'; the integrator may prefer 'Kammerberg Spätburgunder' in plan.json.
The VDP says the site was rediscovered in 1965 by Friedrich Becker without saying which; the record says the Beckers.

changed: story: the cooperative founded by the village growers after the war is cut, found in no source of this check; the mixed farm until the 1970s and the wine sold to the village cooperative stand on two accounts.

story and cards[1]: stopped selling grapes to the cooperative is now left the cooperative, the words of the estate and two accounts; the fox is drawn from one of Aesop's fables, as the estate tells it.
story: the Wechsellagen, vineyards that changed their nationality so often, are cut, found in no source of this check.

story, traps[0] and questions[0]: grapes from the French side may be sold as German wine, though not the other way round, is now that the Kammerberg is a parcel of the Sonnenberg on its French side whose wine is made at Schweigen and sold as Pfalz, the VDP's listing; Meininger reports a court dispute over how such labels may name a French parcel and an EU rule that may call for other words, so the legal claim and the reverse rule are cut.

wine.making and table: open vats are now open wooden vats with the cap punched down each day, and young barriques are French oak barriques for up to twenty months, the estate's own red wine pages.

others[1]: the Heydenreich, another Grosse Lage of Schweigen, is now another of the estate's Grosse Lage sites for Pinot Noir, the VDP's estate page, which does not place it in Schweigen.
